8f5bf0a259c9901faaa6.text: A sentence expressing condition and its result is called conditional sentence. Basically, it is composed of two clauses. The subordinate clause also known as the “if”- clause and the main clause or result clause.

86f96dd6d4715783b6fe.text: Conditional sentence type 3 talks about unreal situation in the past. It is contrary to the fact; things which did not happen in the past and impossible to be fulfilled. This type of conditional sentence is used to express regret or criticism.

rows: IF-CLAUSE
RESULT-CLAUSE
1. If I had phoned you last night,
I would have reminded you to stay.
2. If it had rained hard,
I might have not visited your place.
3. If she had taken her medicine,
she could have felt better.
2c7cb504c8feae56cbc1.text: IF-CLAUSE RESULT-CLAUSE 1. If I had phoned you last night, I would have reminded you to stay. 2. If it had rained hard, I might have not visited your place. 3. If she had taken her medicine, she could have felt better.

5eaf29342f5d51ace249.text: If the “if”-clause comes first, a comma (,) is usually used. However, if it comes after the main clause, no need for a comma.

50bfbd9475e192bd57e1.text:  If you had listened to my advice, you would have finished your

ef18623a2ed7085ea639.text:
homework.
 You would have finished your homework if you had listened to my advice.

rows: IF-CLAUSE
RESULT-CLAUSE
If + Past Perfect (If + had + past participle)
subject +would have + past participle could have might have should have
1. If I had phoned you last night, 2. If it had rained hard, 3. If she had taken her medicine,
I would have reminded you to stay. I might have not visited your place. she could have felt better.

If I had phoned you last night, 2. If it had rained hard, 3. If she had taken her medicine, I would have reminded you to stay. I might have not visited your place. she could have felt better.
